paragraphs: Suitable for a first try: willing to start conversations with unfamiliar customers proactively and answer their questions, able to accept continuous standing and moving around the venue rather than a fixed workstation, willing to explain a product's features, price, and usage limits truthfully without exaggeration, able to stay polite and patient when customers rush or crowd around, and willing to record demonstrations and sales per the rules and keep the display area tidy.

Needs caution: if you dislike repeatedly striking up conversations with strangers, find it hard to accept long periods of standing and demonstrating the same product repeatedly, tend to lose patience when customers question or refuse, or are inclined to exaggerate effects or conceal limitations to close a purchase, the actual work will not match expectations and may run into advertising compliance risk.

The core output is truthful, traceable demonstration and promotion: demonstration explanations and Q&A prepared from product materials, records accurately explaining features, price, and usage limits to customers, registration of samples and materials handed out, records of sales and demonstration feedback, and records of handling and escalating display and on-site anomalies, rather than simply that the product was sold.

Low-risk verification: using public or fictional materials, complete one exercise—write a three-minute product demonstration script and list three questions customers might ask, rewrite a product information sheet as one page of accurate selling points and limitations, and write a demonstration record and anomaly escalation process—and judge only work preferences; the exercise does not use real brand materials, real customer information, or real sales promises, and does not equal job training completion or a hiring promise.

Decision center: whether, with product facts, price and offer authorization, customer questions and refusal, display and on-site conditions, and recording and escalation rules all present at once, one can turn demonstration preparation, live explanation and Q&A, sales and records, display maintenance, and anomaly handling into a truthful, compliant, traceable promotion loop.

The work is mainly in stores, booths, and event sites, requiring long periods of standing, frequent walking, and moving demonstration materials, with emotional and scripting pressure from peak traffic, customer refusal, and sales targets; product categories, demonstration formats, pay methods, and recording requirements differ noticeably across employers (professional, scientific, and technical services, manufacturing, retail trade, and others).

Similar names for adjacent positions do not mean the same duties; when comparing, first check whether the object is in-store product demonstration and promotion, counter and rental business, after-sales and inquiry response, overall store display and window arrangement, parts sales, routine store retail, business-to-business service and wholesale sales, warehouse restocking and order picking, or telephone sales, and whether the position includes sales commission, demonstration authorization, or the authority to publish promotional content externally.

Product materials, price and offer authorization, and demonstration process and recording requirements can be treated as inputs that must be verified, but one must not make unverifiable statements about a product's effects, price, or safety, must not pose as an independent experience or conceal an interest relationship with the brand, and must not continue demonstrating while displays are unstable, samples are scattered, or the site is crowded without dealing with it.

Fit judgments should combine mentored observation in real demonstration settings, feedback from the store or brand, and customer communication records, and are not replaced by an interest type or a single test.

All paper exercises on this page use fictional materials; in real work, product promotion, price and offers, sample distribution, sales and invoicing, and customer information handling must follow the applicable rules on consumer protection and advertising, product and food safety requirements, venue safety rules, and employer and brand policy, and demonstrations involving food, cosmetics, or electrical appliances must also meet the safety and labeling requirements for the corresponding category.

values: Fictional demonstration and promotion scenario material (exercise input)

Fictional scenario: an in-store demonstrator encounters four problems during the same promotion. First, a customer asks whether an effect is supported by third-party testing, but the product materials do not say; second, a customer asks to settle at a ten percent discount, but the day's authorization only goes as far as five percent; third, a trial sample is knocked over and scattered on the demonstration table, and the floor is slippery; fourth, a customer hopes the product can be used for children, but the materials do not state the applicable age.
Provided materials: product materials and the authorized offer scope; the demonstration process and on-site safety standards; sales and demonstration record forms.

Not provided: whether the effect can be described as third-party tested, whether a discount beyond authorization can be requested, whether the demonstration must be paused when samples are scattered and the floor is slippery, and whether one can answer that it can be used for children when the materials do not state the applicable age. If these conditions are needed in the exercise, state your assumptions and the party you need to confirm with.
Task requirements

Write a one-page handling and escalation plan: including how to respond to and verify the question about the effect, how to handle a discount beyond authorization, on-site handling when a sample is scattered and the floor is slippery, and how to answer and record when the materials do not state the applicable age.

The plan must state which information comes from the prompt materials and which is still an assumption, and explain whether it relies on the product materials and authorized offer scope, the demonstration process and on-site safety standards, or the sales and demonstration record forms.
Reference deliverable (derivable from the prompt)

The plan should include: effect (when the materials do not state whether there is third-party testing, do not endorse testing or the effect, explain that the responsible person must confirm before answering, and do not guess), discount (when the day's authorization only goes as far as five percent, do not promise a ten percent discount, ask the responsible person whether it can be requested, and keep the communication record), on-site safety (when a sample is scattered and the floor is slippery, pause the demonstration first, clean up and put the samples back, place a warning, and continue only after safety is confirmed), applicable age (when the materials do not state the applicable age, do not answer affirmatively, explain that it must be verified and suggest the customer refer to the instructions or ask the responsible person), and records (state the status of the four items, the actions taken, and the items pending confirmation).
The reference deliverable lists only the elements that should be included; it does not require wording identical to the example, and it is enough to explain the basis for the judgment.
Boundaries and conclusions that cannot be inferred

This exercise only tests awareness of truthful statements, authorization boundaries, on-site safety, and records; it does not evaluate whether handling in real promotion is compliant, and does not constitute compliance, safety, or legal advice.

Real brand materials, real customer information, and real sales promises must not be used; where real product promotion, price and offers, sample distribution, and customer information handling are involved, this must follow the applicable consumer protection and advertising rules, product and food safety requirements, venue safety rules, and unit policy, and obtain brand authorization or the relevant certificates when necessary.

entries.answer: Demonstrates goods and answers customer questions to raise purchase interest, and may also sell the demonstrated product: providing samples, coupons, or promotional materials to customers; selling and keeping sales records; keeping the area tidy and putting items back after the demonstration; demonstrating or explaining goods, methods, or services; recording and reporting demonstration-related information; making purchase suggestions based on customer needs; researching the product in advance; setting up displays and the demonstration area; identifying interested customers; traveling to trade shows, stores, or other venues to demonstrate and answer questions; moving, assembling, and disassembling demonstration materials; rehearsing the demonstration; learning about competitors or customer concerns; guiding customers in modifying the product; collaborating with the demonstration team at large events; adjusting the demonstration content for a specific audience; restocking shelves; providing product information through explanation, films, charts, or slides; training other demonstrators; suggesting improvements to the employer's goods or services; and walking around public places in costumes or signs to promote goods, services, or events.
entries.question: What does a demonstrator and product promoter do in a typical day?

entries.answer: The core of this occupation is demonstrating goods in stores, booths, or at event sites and answering customer questions to raise purchase interest and prompt immediate purchase or trial; retail salespersons center on routine store reception, sales, and checkout; merchandise displayers and window trimmers center on visual display and spatial arrangement; service sales representatives sell service solutions to business customers; wholesale and manufacturing sales representatives do bulk sales to institutional customers; counter and rental clerks handle counter or rental procedures; telemarketers promote through outbound telephone calls. Similar names do not mean duties, evaluation standards, or assessment methods are interchangeable.

entries.answer: Product material assistants, script generation, and feedback aggregation can help organize materials, draft talking points, and aggregate customer questions; but a tool-generated script does not mean the product facts are accurate, and promotional talking points do not equal truthful statements within authorization—verifying features and usage limits, explaining price and offers within authorization, answering on-site customer questions about the physical product, observing and responding to customer reactions, handling samples and on-site safety, and recording sales and demonstration information still fall to people, and technical capability does not equal truthful content, compliant promotion, or employer adoption. O*NET shows that in this occupation 26% say being accurate and precise is extremely important, 67% say dealing with external customers or the public is extremely important, and 50% have a lot of freedom in how to make decisions; technical exposure does not equal organizational adoption or job disappearance, and cannot be interpreted as a probability of job loss.
entries.question: How will AI affect or replace demonstrators and product promoters?

entries.answer: What can be verified is change at the task level: three types of tasks—product material organization and scripting, customer question aggregation and recording, and demonstration format and material production—can be assisted by tools; this page has no adoption rate or substitution data for this single occupation.

entries.answer: Verifying product facts and usage limits, explaining price and offers within authorization, live physical demonstration and customer Q&A, sample and on-site safety, and the completeness of sales and demonstration records.

description.text: Demonstrators and product promoters (O*NET-SOC 41-9011.00) demonstrate goods and answer customer questions to raise public purchase interest in the goods, and may also sell the demonstrated goods: the tasks covered include providing samples and promotional materials, selling and recording, keeping the demonstration area tidy, explaining the goods in a demonstration, recording demonstration-related information, making purchase suggestions, researching the goods in advance, setting up displays and the demonstration area, identifying target customers, traveling to trade shows or stores to demonstrate, moving and assembling demonstration materials, rehearsing the demonstration, learning about competitors and customer concerns, guiding product modification, team collaboration, adjusting content for the audience, restocking, providing information through explanation and audio-visual materials, training other demonstrators, and making improvement suggestions; its U.S. employment and wage definitions must be stated: this occupation is under the O*NET-SOC 41-9011.00 definition for itself, about 79,200 people were employed in 2024, the 2024—2034 projection is essentially unchanged (label little or no change), about 79,100 are projected in 2034, and about 14,000 openings per year over the projection period include growth and replacement; the 2025 wage data shows a median annual wage of 39,320 USD (median hourly 18.91 USD), with annual percentiles of 31,200／35,160／39,320／53,640／63,850 USD; the industries are professional, scientific, and technical services 30%／manufacturing 15%／retail trade 14%／other industries (including wholesale trade) 41%; the interest code is EC and the preparation level is Job Zone 1-2; as well as the occupation-level wage gap for such positions in mainland China and the control points for product fact verification, truthful promotional statements, display and on-site safety, and documentation.

subject.name: Demonstrators and product promoters
subject.summary: In the United States, demonstrators and product promoters correspond to O*NET-SOC 41-9011.00 (Demonstrators and Product Promoters): demonstrating goods and answering customer questions to raise public purchase interest in the goods, and possibly selling the demonstrated goods. The work includes providing customers with samples, coupons, promotional materials, or other incentives to prompt a purchase; selling the promoted goods and keeping sales records; keeping the area tidy during the work and putting items back after the demonstration; demonstrating or explaining goods, methods, or services to persuade customers to buy or use them; recording and reporting demonstration-related information (such as the number of customer questions or coupons distributed); making specific purchase suggestions based on customer needs; researching or learning about the goods to be demonstrated in advance; setting up or arranging displays and the demonstration area to attract potential customers' attention; identifying interested and eligible customers and giving them more information; traveling to trade shows, stores, community organizations, or other venues to demonstrate goods or services and answer questions; moving, assembling, and disassembling materials needed for the demonstration; rehearsing the demonstration to ensure the flow runs smoothly; learning about competitors or customer concerns to answer more completely; guiding customers in modifying the product; collaborating with the demonstration team at large events; adjusting the demonstration content for a specific audience; restocking shelves; providing product information through explanation, films, charts, or slides; training other demonstrators to introduce the company's goods or services; suggesting improvements to the employer's goods or services; and walking around public places in costumes or signs to promote goods, services, or events. The preparation level for this occupation is O*NET Job Zone 1-2 (requiring little to some preparation, SVP below 6.0), and the official education survey shows that among new entrants 64% require a high school diploma or equivalent, 35% require less than high school, and 1% require a master's degree. On O*NET, this subcategory's (41-9011.00) tasks, work context, preparation level, wages, employment, and industry are all its own definition, and the page is not labeled with a parent occupation or an opaque proxy: its national wages page for 2025 wage data publishes both annual and hourly percentiles. Similar positions on the Chinese side are mostly in-store promotion, sales assistant, demonstration, and promotion positions, whose duties and employment and pay definitions are not one-to-one counterparts of this U.S. occupation subcategory and cannot be interchanged.
